standard.title: Adapting and subverting text structures
standard.description: examine how authors adapt and subvert text structures and language features by experimenting with spoken, written, visual and multimodal elements, and their combination
standard.prior_knowledge: Students identify and describe how text structure and language features vary by purpose (AC9E7LA03). They have not yet examined how authors deliberately adapt or subvert expected structures for artistic or rhetorical effect.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine how authors adapt and subvert text structures and language features through experimentation with spoken, written, visual and multimodal elements.

nodes.label: Expected vs adapted structures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify when an author has adapted a conventional text structure and describe what the expected structure would have been.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one text that departs from conventional structure for its genre and describe what the conventional structure looks like.
nodes.typical_width: Compare two texts in the same genre (e.g. two short stories, two feature articles) where one follows convention and one adapts it, explaining how each makes different structural choices.
wider: Examine how digital and multimodal texts (e.g. interactive journalism, social media narratives) extend or adapt print conventions
Analyse how non-linear narrative structures in short fiction create different reading experiences from linear structures

response_modes.reason: Students need exposure to a range of conventional structures before they can recognise adaptation. Building a repertoire of 'what the convention looks like' in different genres is prerequisite to analysing deviation.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot articulate the conventional structure have no baseline against which to identify adaptation or subversion at N2 and N3 — they cannot explain the effect of deviation without knowing what was deviated from.
success_criteria: Student names the conventional structure for the genre
Student identifies at least one structural feature that the text has adapted or departed from

nodes.label: Purpose and effect of structural adaptation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine why an author adapts structure and explain the purpose and effect of the structural choice on the reader.
nodes.minimum_width: Examine one structural adaptation (e.g. non-linear narrative, subverted opening) and explain its purpose and effect on the reader.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse structural adaptations across at least two text types, explaining both the purpose of each adaptation and its effect on meaning or reader response.
wider: Compare how the same structural device (e.g. in medias res opening, fragmented timeline) is used for different purposes across different genres
Examine how public texts such as feature articles use structural experimentation in their opening paragraphs to position readers, and evaluate the effect of these choices

response_modes.reason: Students often describe structural features without connecting them to purpose and effect. The reasoning chain 'structural choice → authorial purpose → reader effect' needs explicit scaffolding — especially for the move from describing what is unusual to explaining why and to what end.

success_criteria: Student explains why an author may have chosen a non-standard structure for this text and context
Student identifies a specific effect the structural choice has on the reader or the text's meaning

nodes.label: Subversion across modes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine how authors subvert conventions by experimenting with the combination of spoken, written, visual and multimodal elements.
nodes.minimum_width: Examine a multimodal text and identify how it subverts or experiments with the combination of at least two modes (e.g. spoken and visual, written and image), explaining the effect.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how structural subversion operates across spoken, written, visual and multimodal elements in a range of texts, including how the combination itself becomes the subversive device.
wider: Analyse how spoken word poetry or performance poetry subverts the conventions of both written poetry and spoken language simultaneously
Examine how digital storytelling experiments with navigation and reader agency as a structural subversion of linear narrative

response_modes.reason: Examining subversion across modes requires students to coordinate understanding of conventions in multiple modes simultaneously — written, spoken, visual — and recognise that the combination itself can be the subversive move. This integration is harder than analysing each mode separately.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multimodal subversion is rich territory for Y9: the elaborations explicitly name spoken, written, visual and multimodal as four sites of structural experimentation. Advancing students can explore how medium and mode expectations interact — a rich conceptual space that stays firmly within Y9 scope.
success_criteria: Student identifies which conventions are being subverted and in which mode(s)
Student explains the effect of the subversive choice on the text's meaning or audience experience
